raw_response:
I've been farming this land for 55 years now. I'm 76, and my wife and I are the only ones left at home — our children work in Shijiazhuang and only come back for the harvest if they can get leave. We have 21.4 mu, which is more than two old people can really manage alone, so I hire labor for the heavy work and the picking. It costs me, but at my age, what choice do I have? My back isn't what it used to be.

It's April now, so the winter wheat I planted last October is already up and green. I put the base fertilizer down before planting — compound fertilizer and some urea — about 20 kg of nitrogen per mu in total. I already topdressed with another round of urea at jointing in March when the extension guy came by. The wheat looks decent, maybe 450 kg per mu if we don't get a late drought. I'll irrigate it once more when the grain is filling, probably in mid-May. The pump electricity isn't cheap, but I've seen what happens when you let wheat go thirsty at heading — you lose more than the irrigation cost. I hire a combine for harvest in early June. I can't run a combine, and neither can my wife.

The real headache every year is that week after wheat harvest. As soon as the combine leaves, I need to get the summer maize in the ground within a few days. The window is tight — sometimes less than a week. I plant hybrid maize seed, about 55 yuan per mu. I don't have time to till, so I direct seed into the wheat stubble. I put compound fertilizer down at planting, roughly 8-10 kg of nitrogen equivalent, and then I topdress with urea when the maize has 7-8 leaves. I'll irrigate twice if it's dry — once around knee-high and once at tasseling. I used to try to save money by irrigating once, but I got burned in 2015 when the August heat hit and the yield was terrible. Now I don't take that chance. I hire a machine to harvest in late September. I expect about 480 kg per mu.

For cotton, I have about 6 mu. I plow and harrow in mid-April — my neighbor brings his small tractor over and I pay him for the diesel. I use hybrid cotton seed, about 45 yuan per mu. Base fertilizer goes in before planting, around 15 kg nitrogen per mu total, plus some phosphorus and potassium. I topdress when the flowers start coming. Cotton needs water at planting and again at flowering, so that's two irrigations. I spray for weeds and bollworm — I've learned you can't skip the insecticide on cotton. The picking is what kills me. My wife and I can pick maybe a little bit, but our fingers ache after an hour. I hire women from the village for the main picking. I expect about 280 kg of seed cotton per mu if the bollworm doesn't get bad.

Chili is on 5 mu. I buy seedlings and transplant in late April. Chili needs more fussing than the other crops — I plow, make ridges, and put plastic mulch down to keep moisture in and weeds out. The mulch costs money, but it saves on weeding labor later. I give chili more potassium than the grains because I've noticed it helps the fruit set. Total nitrogen is about 16 kg per mu, split three times: base, at flowering, and when the fruits are setting. I irrigate four times through the season. Chili gets aphids and sometimes root rot, so I spray insecticide and fungicide. Picking goes on for months — green chilis first, then red ones. I hire labor for most of the picking. I hope for around 1000 kg per mu of fresh chili, but it varies a lot with the weather.

Money is always tight. Seed, fertilizer, pesticide, hired labor, irrigation pumping — it all adds up to nearly 19,000 yuan. I could save some by cutting back on fertilizer or doing more picking myself, but at my age I just can't bend down all day anymore. And I'd rather apply a bit more fertilizer than risk a bad yield — a bad year hurts more than a good year helps. I've seen enough bad years to know.

decision.reasoning_summary: At 76 years old with just my wife and me at home, I have to balance what I know works against what my body can still do. I've been farming for 55 years and I trust my experience — I know this soil and I know that cutting corners on fertilizer or irrigation costs more in lost yield than it saves in cash. But I also know I can't pick cotton or chili all day anymore, so I hire village labor even though it hurts my pocket. My wheat-maize double crop on 10 mu is my foundation — it's mechanized and reliable. The 6 mu of cotton and 5 mu of chili bring in cash but they're labor-hungry. I play it conservative: I'd rather spend a bit more on inputs than risk a bad year, because at my age I don't have time to recover from a big loss.
